I will keep my main land in the wheat-maize rotation and only keep a smaller block for cotton. On 16.9 mu, I care first about steady grain output and not stretching family labor too hard, because some people in my household work off-farm. I have 30 years of experience and well irrigation, so I will lean on the system I know best: irrigated wheat followed by summer maize on most of the land. That gives me the most reliable annual return in my conditions. I will put 12.0 mu into winter wheat and then summer maize on that same 12.0 mu, and I will leave 4.9 mu for cotton to keep some diversification and cash income. For seed, I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize, because I want stable emergence, better yield, and less risk. For cotton, I will also use better seed rather than old saved seed, because I need stronger stand and cleaner bolls.

For fertilizer and field work, I will stay moderate and practical. I will not chase extreme yield with excessive fertilizer, because input costs matter and my land has irrigation support. Wheat will get enough nitrogen to push tillering and grain filling, with phosphorus for roots and some potassium for strength; I will irrigate around key growth stages. Maize will get slightly higher nitrogen because it responds well after wheat, and I will use no-tillage after wheat harvest to save time and labor in the tight summer window. Cotton needs more field watching, so I will keep its area smaller, give it balanced fertilizer with a bit more potassium, irrigate several times through flowering and boll setting, and spray more often than grain crops because insects are usually a bigger problem there. My goal is not the highest possible yield on paper; it is a steady, manageable year with reliable output from wheat and maize and supplemental income from cotton.
